title: Fund Managers Unlock More Investments Toward Clean Energy | BloombergNEF
gist: BNEF's 2026 Energy Supply Fund Ratio shows public-market funds' portfolio companies spent $0.80 on low-carbon energy supply per $1 of fossil capex at end-2025 (up from 0.73 in early 2024), still short of net-zero levels. Credit funds (1.2) and private markets (just over 1.2) tilt cleaner than equity funds (0.7), while passive S&P 500 trackers dominated by Vanguard and BlackRock limit managers' ability to steer the ratio.

insights.claim: Among companies held by public-market funds, $0.80 of low-carbon energy supply capex was enabled for every $1 of oil, gas and coal capex at end-2025, per BNEF's Energy Supply Fund Ratio (ESFR).
insights.speaker: BloombergNEF
insights.so_what: Fund-held corporate energy capex is approaching parity between clean and fossil; parity (1.0) is a watchable milestone for transition-themed allocators.
insights.locator: Among the companies held by public

insights.claim: The ESFR for public-market pooled vehicles rose to 0.8 in 2025 from 0.73 at the beginning of 2024, a multi-year rising trend.
insights.speaker: BloombergNEF
insights.so_what: Steady upward drift signals structural reallocation of corporate capex toward low-carbon supply, not a one-off.
insights.locator: Company spending tilts toward clean energy

insights.claim: Despite its rise, the 0.8 fund-enabled clean-to-fossil capex ratio remains below the level BNEF says is required to deliver net-zero emissions.
insights.speaker: BloombergNEF
insights.so_what: Gap to net-zero-consistent ratios implies further capex shift is needed, supporting long-run demand for clean supply chains and pressure on fossil-heavy holdings.
insights.quote: That ratio has been rising for the past few years, but it’s still short of the level that would deliver net-zero emissions.
insights.locator: Among the companies held by public

insights.claim: The rise in the ESFR was driven mainly by portfolio companies increasing low-carbon capex relative to fossil capex, not by fund managers reallocating.
insights.speaker: BloombergNEF
insights.so_what: Improvement is corporate-led; watch company capex guidance (utilities, grids, renewables) as the leading indicator for fund ratios.
insights.locator: The main driver was a rise

insights.claim: Accelerating power-grid spending translated into $36 billion of fund-enabled capex in 2025.
insights.speaker: BloombergNEF
insights.so_what: Grid capex is a key growth leg of clean-energy spending, supporting grid equipment and utility names.
insights.locator: The main driver was a rise

insights.claim: BNEF's ESFR covers more than 85,000 exchange-traded, mutual and private-market funds and measures capex enabled in low-carbon assets versus fossil fuels; it sits within BNEF's suite of Energy Supply Ratios tracking financial institutions' climate progress.
insights.speaker: BloombergNEF
insights.so_what: A reusable metric for screening managers and funds on transition alignment by enabled capex rather than holdings-based emissions.

insights.claim: Vanguard and BlackRock enabled more energy capex through public-market funds than the remaining top-10 largest asset managers combined, and both managers' ESFRs stayed relatively flat over 2025.
insights.speaker: BloombergNEF
insights.so_what: The two giants effectively set the aggregate public-market clean/fossil capex mix; their flat ratios cap how fast the industry average can move.

insights.claim: European and Asian asset managers run higher clean-to-fossil capex ratios than American peers but enable considerably less capex in absolute terms.
insights.speaker: BloombergNEF
insights.so_what: Cleanest portfolios are not where the capital scale is; absolute capital influence remains US-centric.

insights.claim: Most fund capital supporting energy investment sits in large diversified broad-index trackers, and S&P 500 tracker funds make up half of the 10 largest funds by enabled capex.
insights.speaker: BloombergNEF
insights.so_what: Index composition, not manager discretion, largely determines how fund capital supports energy capex.
insights.locator: Tracker funds give managers less influence

insights.claim: The S&P 500's ESFR fell in 2025 because of index membership changes: natural gas producer Expand Energy joined while renewable equipment maker Enphase Energy exited after its market cap fell.
insights.speaker: BloombergNEF
insights.so_what: Index inclusions/exclusions mechanically shift trillions in passive exposure between fossil and clean names; market-cap declines in clean stocks compound via index exits.

insights.claim: Passive fund managers have limited influence over their ESFRs because they must mirror index constituent changes.
insights.speaker: BloombergNEF
insights.so_what: Engagement/ratio pressure on passive giants has limited effect; clean-capex flows depend on company fundamentals and market cap.
insights.quote: This illustrates the limited influence managers have on ESFRs for passive funds.

insights.claim: High-ESFR funds exist but are typically thematic strategies holding considerably less capital, though their inflows have picked up since 2025.
insights.speaker: BloombergNEF
insights.so_what: Recovering inflows to clean thematic funds are a sentiment signal for clean-energy equities, but remain small relative to passive pools.

themes.theme: Credit and private markets tilt clean

insights.claim: Credit funds enable $1.20 of low-carbon capex for every $1 going to fossil fuels, versus an overall ratio of 0.7 for equity funds.
insights.speaker: BloombergNEF
insights.so_what: Fixed income is already past parity; bond investors are the more clean-aligned capital pool.

insights.claim: Credit funds skew cleaner because lower-carbon companies typically take on more debt than fossil-fuel companies to fund upfront capex on assets like wind and solar farms.
insights.speaker: BloombergNEF
insights.so_what: Clean energy's capital intensity makes it rate- and credit-sensitive; debt markets are a key transmission channel for the transition.
insights.quote: Lower-carbon companies typically take on more debt than fossil-fuel companies to pay upfront for assets like wind and solar farms.

insights.claim: Fixed income and private-market funds have higher ESFRs than listed equity funds but support less total energy spending.
insights.speaker: BloombergNEF
insights.so_what: Cleanest asset classes are smaller; listed equity still drives the bulk of enabled energy capex.

insights.claim: Private markets are the asset class with the highest ESFRs, at just over 1.2, and institutional ratios vary widely among large private managers, offering more choice than public-market leaders.
insights.speaker: BloombergNEF
insights.so_what: Allocators seeking clean-energy exposure have more differentiated manager selection options in private markets.

insights.claim: Newer private-market funds tilt more toward clean energy and hold more dry powder, which BNEF expects to keep private-market ESFRs above other asset classes.
insights.speaker: BloombergNEF
insights.so_what: Undeployed private capital skewed to clean energy points to continued private funding of renewable and grid assets.
insights.quote: This should continue to support higher private market ESFRs relative to other asset classes.
